title: Military freezers become a suspected target
summary: Refrigeration failures affected at least six military commissaries and were investigated as a suspected cyberattack. NPR's November 3 review of public contracts found Danfoss controllers installed at some affected bases. Which equipment was compromised, the attack method, and any connection to Europe's attacks remain unconfirmed.

title: Supermarket fridges forced into defrost
summary: An overnight wave disrupted supermarket refrigeration and spoiled stock. France's CERT confirmed numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. On November 9, France officially attributed the October 11–12 campaign to Iran’s Shahid Kaveh unit, affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The accompanying C4 report describes about 700 affected retail sites and at least 15 fire outbreaks. This attribution concerns the October campaign; it does not establish responsibility for the November incidents.

title: The attacks extend beyond Danfoss
summary: Further reporting described attacks on Dixell equipment. CERT-FR expanded its alert to include Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB controllers. This is a continuation of the October wave.

title: Another wave. More spoiled food.
summary: Refrigeration attacks were reported in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden, with some settings raised to 50°C. Follow-ups described contemporaneous incidents in Germany, Portugal and Sicily; some affected systems used Danfoss controllers. Greece acknowledged domestic food-retail attacks on November 3 without incident dates or an established link to this wave. Finland reported suspected domestic incidents on November 3 and refrigeration-related damage on November 6, without incident dates or controller vendors. Separately, Ransom-ISAC’s November 6 analysis of an anonymized November 2 Copeland XWEB log describes configuration changes across 31 listed devices; actual temperatures, stock loss and a connection to other attacks remain unconfirmed. Claims of responsibility by NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest were reported on November 4 and remain independently unverified. A common perpetrator is unconfirmed, and these follow-ups do not establish a distinct new wave.

title: Blood-service cold storage is affected
summary: EFS confirmed that a refrigeration supplier incident altered cold-room temperature and defrost settings at three sites. Alarms enabled staff to secure equipment or transfer plasma; no product losses or health impact were reported, and collection and distribution continued. EFS did not identify the supplier or controller vendor. A link to the supermarket attacks remains unconfirmed. Separately, Coolworld’s November 4 statement acknowledged an early-November remote-monitoring incident affecting a limited number of its units and described a third-party component vulnerability. It declined to discuss individual customer cases; this does not establish which controller or access route was involved at EFS.
